title: Cybersecurity
description: A defensive course on how systems are attacked and protected, from risk and threat modelling to web security, identity, cryptography and incident response.
audience: A capable adult with basic computing and networking knowledge, who may have tried hands-on labs such as Kali exercises but not studied the foundations. Practice is described only in authorised labs.
outcomes: You'll be able to classify a failure by confidentiality, integrity or availability and justify a control with annualised loss.
You'll be able to threat model a small system with STRIDE.
You'll be able to read a firewall rule set, a port scan and a log for signs of attack.
You'll be able to recognise injection, broken access control, CSRF and SSRF and name the fix.
You'll be able to judge a password scheme, a token and a certificate chain.
You'll be able to run the first hour of an incident by the NIST lifecycle.

modules.title: Foundations and threats
modules.summary: What security protects, how risk is reasoned about, how to model a system's threats, and how attacks proceed.

modules.title: Network and web security
modules.summary: How networks are segmented and defended, and the classes of flaw that most often break web applications.

modules.title: Identity and cryptography
modules.summary: Proving who someone is, deciding what they may do, and the cryptographic tools underneath.

modules.title: Vulnerabilities and response
modules.summary: Finding and fixing weaknesses, seeing attacks in logs, and handling an incident by the book.

lessons.title: What security protects
lessons.objective: Name confidentiality, integrity and availability, classify a failure by which it breaks, and compute annualised loss to justify a control.

concepts.title: CIA triad
concepts.summary: Confidentiality (only authorised readers), integrity (no unauthorised change) and availability (usable when needed).

concepts.title: Risk
concepts.summary: The combination of how likely a harmful event is and how much it would cost.

concepts.title: Annualised loss expectancy
concepts.summary: Single loss expectancy multiplied by annual rate of occurrence.

misconceptions: Security is about keeping attackers out; it also covers accidents, failures and insiders, and availability is part of it.
All risk should be removed; the aim is to reduce it to an acceptable level at justified cost.
A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is still worthwhile because security matters; it must be justified.
sequence: Open on three incidents: a leaked customer list, an altered invoice, a ransomware outage; each breaks one property.
Define the triad and add authentication and non-repudiation as related ideas.
Define threat, vulnerability, asset and risk.
Compute ALE and compare a control's cost with its saving.
Frame the NIST CSF 2.0 functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) as the course map.
examples: A breach costing $40,000 expected twice every four years (rate 0.5) gives an ALE of 40,000 x 0.5 = $20,000. A $15,000 control cutting the rate to 0.1 leaves an ALE of $4,000, a saving of $16,000, a net gain of $1,000.
Ransomware that encrypts files and halts work breaks availability first, and confidentiality if data is also stolen.

figures.shows: Triangle of the three properties with six incidents.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each incident to the property it breaks.

figures.shows: Asset, threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact rows of a mini risk register.
figures.learnerAction: Edit the likelihood and see the ALE.

questionPlan.sample: An attacker alters the amount on an invoice in transit. Which property is broken?
A loss of $40,000 is expected to occur 0.5 times a year. What is the annualised loss expectancy in dollars?
A control costing $15,000 cuts the rate of the $40,000 loss from 0.5 to 0.1 a year. What is the net annual benefit in dollars?

historyNotes: NIST CSF 1.0 appeared in 2014; version 2.0 (February 2024) added the Govern function.

lessons.title: Threat modelling
lessons.objective: Draw a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries and use STRIDE to list threats and a response to each.

concepts.title: Data-flow diagram
concepts.summary: A picture of processes, data stores, external entities and flows, with trust boundaries where privilege changes.

concepts.title: STRIDE
concepts.summary: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

concepts.title: Mitigation
concepts.summary: A design or control chosen to reduce a threat: remove it, reduce it, transfer it or accept it.

misconceptions: Threat modelling needs a security expert and a finished product; it is cheapest on a sketch and done by the team.
STRIDE lists attacks; it is a prompt for categories of threat, each tied to a property.
Every threat must be fixed; some are accepted with a recorded reason.
sequence: Four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, did we do a good job.
Draw a login-and-orders web app with a browser, server and database.
Mark trust boundaries and apply STRIDE to each flow crossing one.
Map each STRIDE letter to the property it violates.
Record decisions and revisit when design changes.
examples: Spoofing violates authentication; tampering violates integrity; information disclosure violates confidentiality; denial of service violates availability.
The flow browser to server crosses a trust boundary; the flow server to database is inside one, if the database is on a private network.

figures.shows: A DFD for a small web shop with two trust boundaries.
figures.learnerAction: Tap a flow to cycle STRIDE prompts and add a mitigation.

figures.shows: Six STRIDE letters and the property each violates, with blanks.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in the property.

questionPlan.sample: In STRIDE, which letter stands for an attacker pretending to be another user?
Tampering most directly violates which property?
Where should trust boundaries be drawn?
questionPlan.answer: Wherever data crosses between different levels of trust or privilege
choices: Wherever data crosses between different levels of trust or privilege

historyNotes: STRIDE was developed at Microsoft in the late 1990s and published by Kohnfelder and Garg (1999); check the exact citation.

lessons.title: How attacks proceed and how to layer defences
lessons.objective: Describe stages of an intrusion, layer controls against it, and state the limits of legal, authorised practice.

concepts.title: Attack stages
concepts.summary: Reconnaissance, initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement and impact; each gives a chance to detect.

concepts.title: Defence in depth
concepts.summary: Several independent controls, so one failure does not lead to compromise.

concepts.title: Authorisation to test
concepts.summary: Security testing is lawful only with the system owner's written permission and a defined scope.

misconceptions: Attackers use advanced exploits; many intrusions begin with stolen credentials or an unpatched known flaw.
One strong control is enough; each control fails sometimes.
Scanning someone else's network is harmless; without permission it can be illegal.
sequence: Describe a real-style intrusion sequence at a high level.
Introduce ATT&CK as a catalogue of observed techniques.
Layer controls: network, host, application, identity and data, plus detection.
Link layers to stages: what each stage lets a defender catch.
Set ground rules for labs: own machines, CTF games, written scope.
examples: Phishing for credentials gives initial access; a stolen admin token enables lateral movement; encryption of files is impact.
Layers for a customer database: network segment, host patching, application authentication, encryption, audit alerting.

figures.shows: Seven attack stages out of order.
figures.learnerAction: Put them in order.

figures.shows: Concentric rings (data, application, host, network, perimeter) with a failing ring.
figures.learnerAction: Disable one ring; see which layers still hold.

questionPlan.sample: Which attack stage comes first?
Why use defence in depth?
questionPlan.answer: Because any single control can fail
choices: Because any single control can fail
It removes the need for logging

questionPlan.sample: What do you need from the owner before testing a system you do not own?

lessons.title: Network security
lessons.objective: Read a firewall rule set and a port-scan result, and choose segmentation and wireless settings.

concepts.title: Firewall rule
concepts.summary: An ordered allow or deny decision on source, destination, port and protocol; the first match wins and a default deny ends the list.

concepts.title: Network segmentation
concepts.summary: Splitting a network into zones so a compromised host cannot reach everything.

concepts.title: Exposed service
concepts.summary: A listening port reachable by others; each one is attack surface.

misconceptions: A firewall at the edge protects the inside; internal segmentation and host controls matter because attackers get in through phishing.
Open ports are vulnerable ports; they are surface, and risk depends on the service and its patch level.
Hidden Wi-Fi names or MAC filtering secure a network; WPA2 or WPA3 with a strong passphrase does.
sequence: Recall TCP/IP and ports from CS basics.
Read a scan and say what each service is.
Write rules in order with default deny.
Segment: user, server, database and guest zones.
Wireless: WPA2/WPA3, why WEP is broken, and what a deauthentication attack can and cannot do.
examples: 22/tcp ssh, 80/tcp http, 443/tcp https, 445/tcp smb, 3389/tcp rdp, 3306/tcp mysql, 5432/tcp postgres.
Rules: 1 allow tcp 443 from any to web; 2 allow tcp 5432 from web to db; 3 deny all. A packet from any to db on 5432 matches rule 3 and is denied.

figures.shows: Scan output with port, state and service.
figures.learnerAction: Mark which services should not be internet-facing.

figures.shows: Zones with firewalls and a rule table; send a packet.
figures.learnerAction: Add and reorder rules and trace the packet.

questionPlan.sample: A scan of a public web server shows open ports 22, 80, 443 and 3306. Which port is a database that should not face the internet?
Rules in order: 1 allow tcp/443 any to web; 2 allow tcp/5432 web to db; 3 deny all. Does a packet from any host to db on tcp/5432 get allowed? Answer yes or no.
What should the final rule of a firewall rule set be?

lessons.title: Injection and cross-site scripting
lessons.objective: Explain why concatenating input into a query or page is dangerous and fix it with parameters and output encoding.

concepts.title: Injection
concepts.summary: Untrusted input is interpreted as code by a database, shell or browser.

concepts.title: Parameterised query
concepts.summary: The query text and the values are sent separately, so a value can never change the query's structure.

concepts.title: Cross-site scripting
concepts.summary: Attacker-controlled script runs in a victim's browser; output encoding and a content security policy reduce it.

misconceptions: Escaping quotes by hand is a fix; parameters are, because they separate code from data.
Input validation alone prevents injection; it helps but encoding or parameters at the sink is the control.
XSS only matters for alerts; scripts can steal sessions and act as the user.
sequence: Show a login query built with string concatenation.
Enter a name that closes the string and adds a condition.
Run the injected query on a small table.
Show the parameterised form and why it holds.
Show XSS reflecting input into a page and the encoded version.
examples: name = ' OR '1'='1 makes WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1' true for every row, returning all rows.
Encoding turns <script> into <script> so the browser shows text rather than running it.

figures.shows: A users table of 3 rows and the query text as built.
figures.learnerAction: Type a name and see rows returned; switch to parameterised.

figures.shows: A page template with a user comment inserted, raw versus encoded.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle encoding.

questionPlan.sample: Table users has 3 rows. Run: SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'; How many rows come back?
Which is the primary fix for SQL injection?
Which defence best stops stored XSS in a comment page?

lessons.title: Broken access control and forged requests
lessons.objective: Recognise direct-object references, CSRF and SSRF in a request, and say where the server must check.

concepts.title: Broken access control
concepts.summary: A user can act outside their permissions because the server does not check each request.

concepts.title: Cross-site request forgery
concepts.summary: A malicious site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request; same-site cookies and tokens stop it.

concepts.title: Server-side request forgery
concepts.summary: The server is tricked into fetching an attacker-chosen URL, often an internal one.

misconceptions: Hiding a link or button protects the page behind it; the server must check authorisation on every request.
Using POST stops CSRF; the browser still sends cookies on cross-site POST unless a token or SameSite is used.
Unguessable ids are authorisation; they are obscurity, and the check is still required.
sequence: Show /invoices/1042 and change the number.
State the rule: authorise on the server for every object.
Explain how a browser attaches cookies automatically, giving CSRF.
Show SSRF reaching a cloud metadata address or internal service.
List fixes: checks, SameSite, tokens, allowlists for outbound requests.
examples: User 7 requests /invoices/1042 which belongs to user 9; the server returns it: broken access control.
A page fetching a user-supplied URL can be pointed at http://169.254.169.254/, the link-local metadata address on AWS.

figures.shows: Request sequence for a normal and a forged cross-site request.
figures.learnerAction: Step through; toggle SameSite.

figures.shows: Requests with user, object and owner.
figures.learnerAction: Mark which should be denied.

questionPlan.sample: User 7 changes /invoices/1042 to /invoices/1043 in the URL and sees another customer's invoice. This flaw is:
Which cookie attribute helps defend against CSRF?
What does the S in SSRF stand for?

historyNotes: Broken access control was ranked first in the 2021 OWASP Top 10; the list is revised periodically, so quote the current edition.

lessons.title: Passwords and authentication
lessons.objective: Judge a password scheme by search space, store passwords correctly and explain multi-factor authentication.

concepts.title: Search space
concepts.summary: The number of possible secrets; for n symbols of an alphabet of size k it is k^n.

concepts.title: Password hashing
concepts.summary: Store a slow, salted hash of each password so a stolen database does not reveal passwords.

concepts.title: Multi-factor authentication
concepts.summary: Combining something known, held and inherent; phishing-resistant factors bind to the real site.

misconceptions: Complexity rules make passwords strong; length and uniqueness matter more, and NIST advises against forced composition and periodic rotation.
Hashing and encryption are the same; a hash is not reversible and encryption is.
SMS codes are as good as any second factor; they are better than none and weaker than app or hardware keys.
sequence: Compute 8 characters from 62 symbols.
Compare a longer lowercase passphrase.
Describe offline guessing against a stolen hash.
Introduce salt and a slow function (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2).
Add MFA types and phishing-resistant keys.
examples: 62^8 = 218,340,105,584,896 candidates; at 10 billion guesses a second that is about 21,834 seconds, or 6.07 hours.
Four words from a 7,776-word list give 7,776^4 = 3,656,158,440,062,976, about 51.7 bits, against 47.6 bits for 8 random characters from 62.

figures.shows: Guess time against length for several alphabets, log scale.
figures.learnerAction: Add characters and see time rise.

figures.shows: Login: password plus salt through a slow hash into a store.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle salt and see identical passwords differ.

questionPlan.sample: How many possible passwords are there of exactly 8 characters from an alphabet of 62 symbols?
At 10 billion guesses a second, how many hours does 62^8 take to search in full? Give two decimal places.
How should a service store user passwords?

lessons.title: Authorisation, sessions and tokens
lessons.objective: Choose between role and attribute models, secure a session, and explain OAuth and OpenID Connect roles.

concepts.title: RBAC and ABAC
concepts.summary: Role-based control grants permissions by role; attribute-based control decides from user, resource and context attributes.

concepts.title: Session
concepts.summary: State that links later requests to an authenticated user, through a cookie or token.

concepts.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
concepts.summary: OAuth delegates limited access to an API; OpenID Connect adds a standard way to learn who signed in.

misconceptions: OAuth is a login protocol; it authorises access and OpenID Connect adds authentication.
A JWT is secure because it is signed; the signature gives integrity, not secrecy, and the payload is readable.
Logging out client-side ends the session; the server must invalidate it.
sequence: Review authentication versus authorisation.
Compare RBAC and ABAC with a documents example.
Describe a session cookie with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
Walk the authorisation-code flow with roles: user, client, authorisation server, resource server.
Decode a JWT as base64url JSON and note what is checked: signature, expiry, audience, issuer.
examples: A JWT's three parts, header.payload.signature, are separated by two dots; the first two are base64url JSON anyone can decode.
Only the doctor of a patient may read the record, and only during working hours: attributes, suited to ABAC.

figures.shows: Authorisation code flow with four parties and arrows.
figures.learnerAction: Step through; click a token to see its contents.

figures.shows: A decoded JWT with fields and a verified or not column.
figures.learnerAction: Change expiry and see rejection.

questionPlan.sample: A rule says only a patient's doctor may read the record, and only on shift. Which model fits best?
How many dots separate the parts of a signed JWT (header.payload.signature)?
What does a JWT signature provide?

lessons.title: Cryptography basics
lessons.objective: Distinguish symmetric encryption, hashing, signatures and key exchange, and say why you do not invent your own.

concepts.title: Symmetric encryption
concepts.summary: One shared key encrypts and decrypts; fast, with a key distribution problem.

concepts.title: Cryptographic hash
concepts.summary: A fixed-size fingerprint of data that is easy to compute and infeasible to reverse; SHA-256 yields 256 bits.

concepts.title: Asymmetric cryptography
concepts.summary: A public key and a private key, used for key exchange and for signatures.

misconceptions: Hiding the algorithm makes it secure; security should rest on the key (Kerckhoffs's principle).
Encoding such as base64 is encryption; anyone can decode it.
MD5 and SHA-1 are fine for integrity; collisions have been found, so use SHA-256 or better for security.
sequence: Show a Caesar shift and why a small key space falls.
Compute key-space sizes: 2^128.
Define hash properties and show SHA-256 output length.
Explain public-key signatures: sign with private, verify with public.
State the rule: use vetted libraries and modes, never invent crypto.
examples: Caesar shift of 3 turns HELLO into KHOOR; decrypting shifts back by 3.
SHA-256 of hello prints 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824, 64 hexadecimal characters.

figures.shows: A Caesar function and an XOR example with editable input.
figures.learnerAction: Run with different keys and text.

figures.shows: Primitive, key type, purpose, example for six primitives.
figures.learnerAction: Match purposes.

questionPlan.sample: Run: print(5 ^ 3). What is printed?
Run: import hashlib; print(len(hashlib.sha256(b'hello').hexdigest())). What is printed?
Decrypt the Caesar text KHOOR using a shift of 3. What is the plain word?

historyNotes: Kerckhoffs stated his principle in 1883; Caesar's shift cipher is described by Suetonius.

lessons.title: TLS and certificates
lessons.objective: Explain how a TLS connection authenticates the server and protects the data, and diagnose common certificate failures.

concepts.title: TLS
concepts.summary: A protocol giving confidentiality, integrity and server authentication over TCP, using key exchange and then symmetric encryption.

concepts.title: Certificate
concepts.summary: A signed statement binding a public key to a name, issued by a certificate authority.

concepts.title: Chain of trust
concepts.summary: A certificate is trusted when a chain of signatures leads to a root the client already trusts.

misconceptions: The padlock means the site is safe; it means the connection is encrypted to the named site.
TLS uses public-key encryption for the whole session; it uses it for key exchange and signatures, then a fast symmetric key.
A certificate expiring is a minor warning; clients should reject it and services must renew in time.
sequence: Show a browser warning and ask what was checked.
Walk the handshake: hello, certificate, key exchange, finished.
Follow the chain from leaf to intermediate to root.
List failures: expired, wrong name, untrusted issuer, revoked.
Mention modern defaults: TLS 1.3, HTTPS everywhere, automatic renewal.
examples: A leaf certificate for shop.example.com signed by Intermediate CA, which is signed by Root CA in the client's trust store: trusted.
A certificate for www.example.com presented for api.example.com fails the name check.

figures.shows: Handshake sequence between browser and server.
figures.learnerAction: Step through; remove the certificate to see failure.

figures.shows: Three-link certificate chain.
figures.learnerAction: Click a link to see issuer and subject.

questionPlan.sample: A certificate for www.example.com is presented for api.example.com. Which check fails?

questionPlan.answer: When a chain of signatures leads to a root it already trusts
choices: When a chain of signatures leads to a root it already trusts

questionPlan.sample: What organisation type signs certificates?

historyNotes: TLS 1.3 was published as RFC 8446 in August 2018.

lessons.title: Vulnerabilities and secure development
lessons.objective: Read a CVSS severity, prioritise patching by exposure, and place security checks in the development process.

concepts.title: CVE and CVSS
concepts.summary: A CVE identifies a public flaw; a CVSS score from 0.0 to 10.0 rates its technical severity.

concepts.title: Prioritisation
concepts.summary: Severity is combined with exposure, exploitation evidence and asset value to choose what to fix first.

concepts.title: Secure development lifecycle
concepts.summary: Threat modelling, code review, dependency and secret scanning and testing run through the build, not only at the end.

misconceptions: The highest score is always fixed first; an internet-facing medium flaw under active attack may outrank an isolated critical one.
Scanners find all vulnerabilities; they find known classes and need triage for false positives.
Patching is IT's job; developers own their dependencies.
sequence: Show a CVE entry and its fields.
Give the qualitative bands.
Add exposure and exploitation to ranking.
Place checks in the pipeline: static analysis, dependency scan, secret scan, review.
Report responsibly: coordinated disclosure and a security.txt file.
examples: CVSS qualitative ratings: None 0.0, Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0.
A 9.8 flaw on an isolated test server and a 7.5 flaw on an internet-facing server already exploited in the wild: fix the 7.5 first.

figures.shows: Five findings with score, exposure and exploit status.
figures.learnerAction: Drag into patch order.

figures.shows: Delivery pipeline with security checks inserted.
figures.learnerAction: Place each check at a stage.

questionPlan.answer: A 7.5 on an internet-facing server being exploited in the wild
choices: A 9.8 on an isolated test server

lessons.title: Logging and detection
lessons.objective: Decide what to log, read a short log to spot an attack, and measure detection speed.

concepts.title: Security logging
concepts.summary: Recording authentication, access, changes and errors with time, actor, action and outcome, without secrets, and protecting the logs.

concepts.title: Detection
concepts.summary: Turning logs into alerts by rules, baselines and correlation, tuned to limit false positives.

concepts.title: Dwell time
concepts.summary: The time between an intruder's start and its detection.

misconceptions: More logging is better; unfocused logs bury the signal and may expose personal data or secrets.
Alerts that fire often are useful; alert fatigue means real events are missed.
An attacker who gets in cannot touch the logs; they delete them, so ship logs elsewhere.
sequence: Show a short authentication log with a burst of failures then a success.
Name what to record and what to keep out.
Write detection rules: threshold, impossible travel, new admin.
Discuss false positives and tuning.
Compute dwell time and why shortening it limits damage.
examples: Twelve failed logins for one account in two minutes from one address, then a success, suggests password guessing that worked.
First malicious activity 09:05 and detection at 14:20 is a dwell time of 5 hours 15 minutes, 315 minutes.

figures.shows: A twenty-line authentication log.
figures.learnerAction: Select the lines that form the attack.

figures.shows: An intrusion timeline with events and detection.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the detection point to see dwell time.

First malicious activity at 09:05 and detection at 14:20 the same day. What is the dwell time in minutes?
Which should never be written to logs?

lessons.title: Incident response
lessons.objective: Lead the first hour of an incident through the NIST lifecycle, and write a blameless review.

concepts.title: Incident lifecycle
concepts.summary: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity (SP 800-61 Rev. 2).

concepts.title: Containment
concepts.summary: Stopping the spread quickly while preserving evidence, before removing the cause.

concepts.title: Post-incident review
concepts.summary: A blameless account of what happened, why, and what changes, with owners and dates.

misconceptions: Wipe the machine first; evidence and scope are lost, and the cause may remain elsewhere.
Incident response starts when an incident happens; preparation (roles, contacts, runbooks, backups) decides how it goes.
Reviews find who to blame; they find which controls and processes failed.
sequence: Open with a ransomware alert at 02:00 and who is called.
Lay out the four phases with examples.
Compare containment options: isolate a host, disable an account, block an address.
Preserve evidence and keep a timeline.
Run a blameless review and update controls; note the 2025 revision aligned with CSF 2.0 functions.
examples: Order: preparation, detection and analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, post-incident activity.
A suspected compromised laptop is isolated from the network (not powered off) to preserve memory while stopping spread.

figures.shows: Four lifecycle phases and example actions.
figures.learnerAction: Sort actions to phases.

figures.shows: A timeline of an incident with decision points.
figures.learnerAction: Choose an action at each point.

questionPlan.sample: What is the first phase of the NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 lifecycle?

historyNotes: SP 800-61 Rev. 2 dates from August 2012; Rev. 3 was released in 2025 aligned to CSF 2.0 (confirm month and structure).

courseCheck: Mixed check: CIA classification, ALE, STRIDE mapping, firewall and scan reading, SQL injection result, search-space arithmetic, JWT structure, cipher outputs, CVSS bands and patch priority, dwell time and incident phase order.
platformNeeds: A sandboxed 'vulnerable query' SQL runner is already possible with relational_query/code-run-sql; no network or exploit tooling is needed.
A threat_model_canvas figure: drag processes, stores and flows, draw trust boundaries and attach STRIDE threats. Fallback: svg_figure plus diagram_choice.
A log_viewer figure: scrollable log lines that the learner can select and tag. Fallback: table.
A packet_path figure for firewall rules with a first-match trace. Fallback: svg_figure with views.
A multi-line monospace block in question prompts for logs and rule sets (code-reading).
unverified: No external site could be reached from the authoring session, so every source has verified false; check URLs, editions and licences.
OWASP Top 10 edition: broken access control was first in 2021; a newer edition may exist and category numbers should be checked.
SP 800-61 Rev. 3 release date and structure; Rev. 2 date August 2012.
CSF 1.0 in 2014 and CSF 2.0 in February 2024 with the Govern function.
NIST SP 800-63B advice on composition and rotation, recalled from memory.
The 169.254.169.254 metadata address is AWS-specific example; the writer should call it an example.
